title: What's been driving Hawaii's lava fountains?
gist: USGS researchers in Science used Kilauea's recent lava fountain episodes, monitored by 35 stations, to test theories of what drives fountains. Eruptions could be predicted from summit tilt, and gas data lean toward a steam-driven model over a carbon dioxide foam model but leave the trigger unexplained.

insights.claim: Lava fountains of several hundred meters occur at only a few hotspot locations such as Mount Etna, Hawaii and Iceland, and what powers them is not yet understood.
insights.speaker: John Timmer

insights.claim: Kilauea has had only three fountaining episodes since 1823 yet is heavily instrumented, with 35 stations carrying seismic, infrasound, geodetic, gas and visual and thermal cameras.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Dense instrumentation makes the recent eruptions an unusually well documented dataset.

insights.claim: After the 2018 eruption partly drained a reservoir, refill accelerated from 2019 with summit inflation above 22 cm a year, doubling to 57 cm a year in 2023 and spreading to a nearby caldera.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Documents the magma recharge preceding the fountaining.

insights.claim: In 2024 a 900-meter fissure sent fountains up to 160 meters high over 13 hours, followed by 52 further fountain eruptions, the most violent exceeding 400 meters.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Scale of the recent eruptive sequence.
insights.locator: In 2024, a large series of earthquakes

insights.claim: Eruptions caused rapid summit deflation followed by slow refilling, and consecutive eruptions occurred at similar summit tilt levels, letting USGS issue alerts despite no clear seismic signal beforehand.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Tilt monitoring offers a practical forecasting approach for hazard management.

insights.claim: One model holds that pressure keeps water dissolved in magma until it flashes to steam at shallow depth, fragmenting the magma so it rises faster and releases more steam until a jet forms.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Competing mechanism that the new data leans toward.

insights.claim: The alternative model holds that carbon dioxide release forms a magma/gas foam at the chamber roof that escapes at a critical point, driving magma out until supply is exhausted.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: The mechanism that the data disfavor.

insights.claim: The new data do not favor a carbon dioxide foam because gas levels stayed low, while sulfur dioxide rose during eruptions but stayed high throughout, so evidence leans toward steam-driven fountains without explaining why a continuous process suddenly triggers them.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Mechanism remains unresolved, so forecasting is still empirical.
insights.quote: So the evidence leans toward the steam-driven eruption model
insights.locator: The new data doesn’t provide a clear picture

insights.claim: Magnesium oxide fluctuated through the cycle, consistent with eruptions depleting a reservoir that is refilled with hot material, while other oxides rose over time, suggesting newly arriving material has a distinct composition.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Chemistry points to changing magma supply.

insights.claim: Infrared gas sampling was hampered by the intensity of infrared during fountaining, and the height of fountains made it unsafe to install more monitoring hardware; one camera was lost capturing images.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Constraints on data quality limit how definitively the mechanism can be established.
insights.quote: One camera notably sacrificed itself in order to bring us images of red-hot, semi-molten rock falling from the sky.
insights.locator: Despite the wealth of nearby sensors
